overview.title: Table 6.1, prior art, and scaling up to overfit
overview.chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning
overview.subsection: 6.2.4 Scaling up: Developing a model that overfits
overview.main_topic: A lookup table of last-layer activations, losses and metrics per task type; using prior art; what it means when you cannot beat a baseline; and the second milestone, deliberately building a model that overfits.
overview.central_idea: Standard task types have standard output configurations (Table 6.1), and most problems have existing templates. If no reasonable architecture beats a baseline, your hypotheses about the data may be false. Once you do have statistical power, find out how much capacity the problem needs by crossing the underfitting/overfitting border: add layers, widen them, train longer.
overview.importance: Table 6.1 is one of the most-used references in the book for configuring a model's output. The section on overfitting states a counterintuitive but central practice: you must overfit first to learn where the ideal capacity lies.
learning_objectives: Choose the last-layer activation, loss and metrics for binary, multiclass single-label, multilabel classification and regression from Table 6.1.
Explain why researching prior art should come before designing from scratch.
State the two hypotheses behind any supervised learning project and what failing to beat a baseline suggests about them.
Explain why the ideal model sits at the border between underfitting and overfitting and why you must cross that border to find it.
List the three ways to make a model overfit.
prerequisites: Sigmoid and softmax outputs, crossentropy and MSE losses (chapter 4)
Optimization vs. generalization, underfitting and overfitting (chapter 5)

summary:
**Table 6.1** (referenced by the loss-function sidebar on p.205) matches task types to output configurations:

| Task | Last-layer activation | Loss | Metrics |
|---|---|---|---|
| Binary classification | Sigmoid | Binary crossentropy | Binary accuracy, ROC AUC |
| Multiclass, single-label | Softmax | Categorical crossentropy | Categorical accuracy, top-k categorical accuracy, ROC AUC |
| Multiclass, multi-label | Sigmoid | Binary crossentropy | Binary accuracy, ROC AUC |
| Regression | None | Mean squared error | Mean absolute error |

The authors then point out that most problems have **existing templates**: you are not the first to build a spam detector, music recommender or image classifier, so research **prior art** to find the feature engineering techniques and architectures most likely to work.

Statistical power is **not always achievable**. If several reasonable architectures fail to beat a simple baseline, the answer may simply not be in the input data. Every project rests on two hypotheses: (1) the outputs can be predicted from the inputs, and (2) the available data is informative enough to learn that relationship. If either is false, go back to the drawing board.

**6.2.4 Scaling up.** With statistical power in hand, ask whether the model is *powerful enough*. A logistic regression model has statistical power on MNIST but is not sufficient to solve it well. The universal tension is between **optimization and generalization**; the ideal model sits right at the border between underfitting and overfitting (undercapacity and overcapacity), and *to find that border you must first cross it*. So deliberately develop a model that overfits, which is easy: **add layers, make the layers bigger, train for more epochs.** (The next page adds: monitor training and validation loss and metrics until validation performance degrades.)

paragraphs.excerpt: Binary classification Sigmoid Binary crossentropy Binary accuracy, ROC AUC Multiclass, single-label
paragraphs.what_it_says: Table 6.1 gives, for four task types, the last-layer activation, loss function and metrics to use: binary classification uses sigmoid, binary crossentropy, binary accuracy and ROC AUC; multiclass single-label uses softmax, categorical crossentropy, categorical accuracy, top-k categorical accuracy and ROC AUC; multiclass multi-label uses sigmoid, binary crossentropy, binary accuracy and ROC AUC; regression uses no activation, mean squared error and mean absolute error.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The activation and loss come as a matched pair. Sigmoid produces an independent probability per output unit, which binary crossentropy compares with a 0/1 target, so it suits both a single yes/no output and multilabel problems where each label is its own yes/no question. Softmax produces one probability distribution over mutually exclusive classes, which categorical crossentropy compares with a one-hot target. Regression leaves the output unconstrained so it can take any real value, and MSE penalizes squared error while MAE, reported in the target's units, is easier to interpret.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Mismatched pairs (softmax for multilabel, sigmoid plus MSE for classification, ReLU on a regression output that can be negative) are common sources of silent failure. The metrics column also reflects the proxy idea from p.205: losses are crossentropies while ROC AUC is monitored.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the difference between single-label and multi-label is whether the classes are mutually exclusive. Softmax forces the probabilities to sum to 1 (one winner); independent sigmoids allow any number of labels to be on at once. In Keras, `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` is the same loss as categorical crossentropy but takes integer labels instead of one-hot vectors (used on p.143).

paragraphs.what_it_says: Most problems have existing templates. Others have built spam detectors, music recommenders and image classifiers before, so research prior art to find the feature engineering techniques and architectures likely to perform well.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Architecture search from scratch is expensive and usually unnecessary. Papers, blog posts, Kaggle solutions and the Keras code examples encode what tends to work for a data type: ConvNets or pretrained vision backbones for images, Transformers for text, gradient-boosted trees or small MLPs for tabular data.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the fastest route to statistical power and sets realistic expectations for what performance is possible.

paragraphs.excerpt: Note that it’s not always possible to achieve statistical power. If you can’t
paragraphs.what_it_says: Statistical power is not always possible. If multiple reasonable architectures cannot beat a simple baseline, the answer may not be present in the inputs. Remember the two hypotheses: the outputs can be predicted from the inputs, and the available data is informative enough to learn the input-output relationship. If they are false, go back to the drawing board.
paragraphs.what_it_means: These are two different failure modes. Hypothesis 1 fails when the target fundamentally does not depend on the inputs: the book's earlier example of predicting stock prices from past prices alone is of this kind. Hypothesis 2 fails when a relationship exists but the dataset is too small, too noisy or missing the key features to reveal it. In both cases more tuning is wasted effort; the fix is in problem framing or data collection.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives you permission, and a criterion, to stop. Not every question is answerable with the data you have, and recognizing that early saves weeks.

paragraphs.excerpt: Once you’ve obtained a model that has statistical power, the question becomes, is
paragraphs.what_it_says: With statistical power achieved, ask whether the model has enough layers and parameters for the problem. Logistic regression has statistical power on MNIST but is insufficient to solve it well. The central tension in ML is optimization versus generalization; the ideal model is right at the border between underfitting and overfitting, between undercapacity and overcapacity. To find that border, you must first cross it.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Beating a baseline only proves the model is learning something. Logistic regression on MNIST reaches roughly 92% accuracy, far above the 10% random baseline, yet a small ConvNet gets over 99%. You cannot know in advance how much capacity is enough, so the only reliable way to locate the sweet spot is to keep increasing capacity until validation performance starts to get worse. That turning point marks the border.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It reverses a beginner's instinct to avoid overfitting at all costs. Overfitting is a diagnostic milestone: a model that cannot overfit is underfitting and has unused potential.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the accuracy figures for logistic regression and ConvNets on MNIST are typical values from common practice, not from this page.

concepts.name: Last-layer activation
concepts.definition: The activation applied to a model's output layer, chosen so the output has the form the loss expects.
concepts.intuition: The output adapter: probabilities for classification, raw numbers for regression.
concepts.technical: Sigmoid: independent per-unit probabilities in (0, 1). Softmax: a distribution summing to 1 across classes. None: unbounded real values.
concepts.significance: Must be paired correctly with the loss (Table 6.1).
concepts.example: A 46-way newswire classifier ends in `Dense(46, activation="softmax")` (p.143).
concepts.misconception: That softmax is right for any multiclass problem; for multi-label tasks you need independent sigmoids.

concepts.name: Loss function choice per task
concepts.definition: Binary crossentropy for binary and multi-label classification, categorical crossentropy for single-label multiclass, MSE for regression.
concepts.intuition: Each loss measures disagreement in the form that matches the output.
concepts.technical: Crossentropy compares predicted probabilities with target labels; MSE penalizes squared differences of real values.
concepts.significance: The loss defines the gradient signal that training follows.
concepts.example: House prices: loss MSE, monitored metric MAE.
concepts.misconception: That the loss and the reported metric must be the same; Table 6.1 lists them separately.

concepts.name: Statistical power and its two hypotheses
concepts.definition: Beating a simple baseline, which presupposes that outputs are predictable from inputs and that the data is informative enough to learn that relation.
concepts.intuition: If no reasonable model can beat guessing, perhaps there is nothing to learn from these inputs.
concepts.technical: Failure after trying multiple reasonable architectures is evidence against one of the two hypotheses.
concepts.significance: Tells you when to stop tuning and revisit problem framing or data collection.
concepts.example: Predicting a fair coin flip from the time of day will never beat 50%.
concepts.misconception: That a bigger model can always find a signal; no model can find information absent from the inputs.

concepts.name: Deliberate overfitting to locate capacity
concepts.definition: Increasing capacity or training time until validation performance starts degrading, to find the border between underfitting and overfitting.
concepts.intuition: To find the edge of a cliff in fog, you have to step just past it.
concepts.technical: Achieved by adding layers, widening layers, or training for more epochs; diagnosed by diverging training and validation curves.
concepts.significance: Second milestone of the universal workflow; prerequisite for regularization and tuning.
concepts.example: Doubling units per layer until validation loss rises after a few epochs while training loss keeps falling.
concepts.misconception: That overfitting is always a failure. Here it is a goal, a measurement of how much capacity is enough.

concepts.name: Model capacity
concepts.definition: The richness of the functions a model can represent, governed mainly by its number of layers and parameters.
concepts.intuition: The size of the model's memory and toolbox.
concepts.technical: Too little capacity means underfitting (cannot fit training data); too much, without regularization, means overfitting.
concepts.significance: The ideal capacity sits at the underfitting/overfitting border.
concepts.example: Logistic regression on MNIST: enough capacity for statistical power, not enough to solve it well.
concepts.misconception: That more capacity always helps; past the border it hurts generalization unless regularized.

deeper.title: Table 6.1 as Keras code
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, an illustrative mapping of the four rows to Keras (not printed on this page):

```python
# Binary classification
layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")
model.compile(loss="binary_crossentropy", metrics=["binary_accuracy", keras.metrics.AUC()])

# Multiclass, single-label (N classes)
layers.Dense(N, activation="softmax")
model.compile(loss="categorical_crossentropy",
              metrics=["categorical_accuracy", keras.metrics.TopKCategoricalAccuracy(k=5)])

# Multiclass, multi-label (N labels)
layers.Dense(N, activation="sigmoid")
model.compile(loss="binary_crossentropy", metrics=["binary_accuracy", keras.metrics.AUC(multi_label=True)])

# Regression
layers.Dense(1)  # no activation
model.compile(loss="mean_squared_error", metrics=["mean_absolute_error"])
```

deeper.title: Why you must cross the border
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, how the procedure plays out in practice:

1. Start from the small model that beat the baseline. Its training and validation losses both decrease and stay close together, so it is probably underfitting.
2. Increase capacity (more units, more layers) or train longer. Repeat while validation loss keeps improving.
3. At some point training loss keeps falling but validation loss bottoms out and rises. You have crossed into overfitting, and the epoch or size at the minimum marks the border.
4. Now you know the scale needed. The next phase (p.207) regularizes this oversized model (dropout, L1/L2, tuning) to move its validation performance back up to, and ideally beyond, the border.

Without step 3 you cannot tell whether a mediocre validation score comes from too little capacity or from something else.

deeper.title: Hypotheses that can fail
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, examples of each hypothesis failing:

- **Outputs not predictable from inputs:** predicting tomorrow's lottery numbers from today's; predicting a stock's future price from its past prices alone (markets largely price in that information).
- **Data not informative enough:** a genuine signal exists, but you have 200 samples of a high-dimensional input, or labels are so noisy that the signal is buried, or a key feature (e.g. weather for retail demand) is missing from the dataset.

The first calls for reframing the problem; the second calls for collecting more or better data, or adding features.

questions.question: Per Table 6.1, what last-layer activation and loss should a multiclass, multi-label classifier use?
questions.explanation: Multi-label means each label is an independent yes/no decision, so per-unit sigmoids with binary crossentropy fit. Softmax plus categorical crossentropy is for mutually exclusive classes. No activation plus MSE is for regression. Softmax plus binary crossentropy is a mismatched pairing.

questions.question: Which loss and which metric does Table 6.1 list for regression?
questions.answer: Loss: mean squared error. Metric: mean absolute error.
questions.explanation: Regression uses no last-layer activation, MSE as the loss, and MAE as the metric, as in the house-price example (p.153).

questions.question: What are the two hypotheses you implicitly make in a supervised learning project, and what does repeated failure to beat a baseline suggest?
questions.answer: (1) Outputs can be predicted given inputs; (2) the available data is informative enough to learn the input-output relationship. Repeated failure with reasonable architectures suggests one of them may be false, and you should go back to the drawing board.
questions.explanation: The page states both hypotheses and says the answer may not be present in the input data.

questions.question: Why does the book say 'to figure out where this border lies, first you must cross it'?
questions.answer: You cannot know in advance how much capacity the problem needs. Only by increasing capacity until validation performance degrades (overfitting) can you see where the optimum between underfitting and overfitting lies.
questions.explanation: The ideal model stands at the border between undercapacity and overcapacity; the turning point of the validation curve is the only empirical marker of that border.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the three ways the page lists to develop a model that overfits?
questions.explanation: Dropout is a regularizer that reduces overfitting; it appears in 6.2.5 (p.207). The other three increase capacity or training time and are the page's bullets.

questions.question: What example does the page use to show that statistical power is not the same as being powerful enough?
questions.answer: A logistic regression model has statistical power on MNIST but would not be sufficient to solve the problem well.
questions.explanation: It beats a trivial baseline, but its capacity is too low to reach strong accuracy.

questions.question: Without looking, fill in Table 6.1's four rows (task, activation, loss, metrics). Then check yourself against the page.
questions.answer: Binary: sigmoid / binary crossentropy / binary accuracy, ROC AUC. Multiclass single-label: softmax / categorical crossentropy / categorical accuracy, top-k categorical accuracy, ROC AUC. Multi-label: sigmoid / binary crossentropy / binary accuracy, ROC AUC. Regression: none / MSE / MAE.
